newsitem.title: ITALY: Bossi slams media, urges calm on Italy "secession".
newsitem.headline: Bossi slams media, urges calm on Italy "secession".

text.p: Separatist Umberto Bossi accused the media on Saturday of peddling lies to the Italian people about his campaign for a new northern state and appealed for calm on the eve of a planned declaration of "independence".

Bossi, on the second leg of a symbol-laden "March to the Sea" along the River Po, Italy's longest river, slammed the press and television as "people who live in their own virtual world where they invent any old rubbish".

The gravel-voiced leader, wearing a boy scout-style green neckchief, arrived late for a key rally in his Northern League party's heartland of Lombardy after river conditions forced him to abandon plans to sail into town on a boat. He drove instead.
A few thousand League supporters gathered in brilliant sunshine to hear Bossi, who leapt up onto one of two flat-bed trucks bedecked with ribbons and flags to speak to the crowd.
The far-right National Alliance party, one of several groups planning events in favour of Italian unity, repeatedly flew a plane overhead trailing a banner proclaiming "Viva L'Italia".

The crowd responded with whistles and shouts of "bastards" and Bossi made several pointed references to it in his speech but there were no reports of trouble. Some 700 left-wing youths pelted League supporters with stones and glass, injuring around 12 people including policemen, after a rally on Friday in Turin.

Bossi reserved most of his venom for the media, whom he accused of lying about the success of the first day of his campaign to liberate "Padania", the name he uses for a vague nation which has no ethnic, linguistic or cultural foundation.

He claimed thousands turned out for the launch of his "March to the Sea" from the Alpine source of the Po with a quasi-religious rite in which he filled a flask with river water to symbolise the birth of his nation.
Witnesses put the number closer to a few hundred. Bossi also said that up to 60,000 people turned out on the banks of the Po in Turin on Friday night but police estimated around 3,000.

The firebrand leader plans to declare "independence" in the lagoon city of Venice on Sunday and predicts millions will flock there for a moment he says will go down in history and which his party likens to the U.S. declaration of independence in 1776.
"Be calm," Bossi urged repeatedly. "The masses arriving tomorrow will make this the biggest political demonstration ever seen in our country." He added: "It must be a peaceful day."

Police wearing riot gear used tear gas to disperse the anti-Bossi protestors on Friday, but no one was badly hurt. In a separate incident, police found a home-made bomb with the words "Viva Bossi" on the Rome-Florence railway. It did not go off.
However Bossi, whose party symbol is a mediaeval warrior holding aloft his sword, said "Padania" was prepared to fight for its rights. "If there must be a battle, so be it," he said.

Former prime minister Silvio Berlusconi, who fell from power when Bossi pulled his party out of the ruling coalition after seven stormy months in 1994, told followers at a counter-rally in Verona that he shared the League's frustrations with high taxes, stifling bureaucracy and public sector inefficiency that have fostered popular discontent in Italy's richest region.
But he warned: "Watch out. The answer does not lie with this secession madness."

Prime Minister Romano Prodi, whose centre-left government is committed to federal reform for Italy, dismissed Bossi's campaign as "a ridiculous game" and said he found "such an artificial event, so little shared by the people" worrying.
Bossi's party won a surprising 10.6 percent in the April general election but a new opinion poll showed only 7.6 percent of Italians favoured secession and 85.6 percent were opposed.

Bossi boarded a catamaran with party officials and some 20 supporters who paid 65,000 lire ($42) for the trip along the Po. His day was due to conclude with a rally in Borgoforte near the mediaeval town of Mantua, seat of his self-styled parliament of the north.
